b: GM Jonas Buhl Bjerre, IM Havard Haug, and GM Jose Martinez were all outright victors of the November 26 3 0 Thursday events, each winning with commanding scores of 10/11.
Bjerre's win was particularly special as it was his first title, and the first by any Danish player. For Haug and Martinez, the victories marked their second and 16th, respectively.
First Tournament: Bjerre, The Cat With Nine Lives
In the first tournament of the day, Bjerre did his best impression of Harry Houdini, somehow escaping from completely lost positions on no less than four occasions.
Bjerre weaseled his way out of trouble against Borischik, Andreikin, Terry, and Tsydypov.

Bjerre almost came unstuck against FM Sergey Borischik in the first round after the latter steered the game into a winning rook and pawn ending. However, Bjerre held on long enough for Borischik's time to become an issue, and flag fall eventually decided the game.
Bjerre (pictured on the right) used the clock as a weapon throughout the entire event. Photo: Maria Emelianova/Chess.com.

In a round six showdown with IM Renato Terry, Bjerre had his closest call. With 2.6 seconds left on the clock, Terry uncharacteristically missed checkmate in one, instead throwing his queen into the line of fire of Bjerre's rooks. Clearly perplexed by the mistake, Bjerre took almost a full second to capture the queen, before also flagging Terry.

One of Bjerre's main challengers was GM Oleksandr Bortnyk, who came face-to-face with the leader in round eight. By this stage, however, the Danish GM was firing on all cylinders. In the late middlegame, he put the game to bed with the astute 34.Rxe7!!.

By the final round, Bjerre had guaranteed a share of first place, and a draw with GM Denis Lazavik confirmed a one-point winning margin. GM Zhamsaran Tsydypov finished in second with 9/11, besting GMs Lazavik and Liem Le on tiebreaks. WIM Meri Arabidze was the top-scoring women's player with 7.5/11.
The top 10 finishers in the first tournament.

Haug's performance in the second tournament was nothing short of breathtaking. He barely put a foot wrong en route to an 8/8 start, frequently capitalizing on opponents' time-pressure-induced mistakes late in the game.
The 16-year-old steamrolled his first eight opponents and then cruised to victory.
Polish GM Zbigniew Pakleza became one of the victims of Haug's opportunism in round three after he blundered a key pawn in an opposite-colored bishop endgame.

In the following game, GM Vladimir Fedoseev was put to the sword in a similar fashion in a rook vs. rook endgame. 16 moves from the 50-move-rule and with 13 seconds on the clock, Fedoseev erred with 98...Rf6??, allowing Haug to acquire an extra half point from the clash.
Having accumulated a half-point lead by the eighth round, Haug played it safe with draws in the ninth and 10th rounds, before asserting his dominance by flagging GM David Paravyan.

With wins in the final round, GM Matthias Bluebaum and FM Dincer Tasdogen finished on 8.5/11 and snuck into second and third place, respectively. Meanwhile, Ukrainian NM Liudmyla Ivanytska secured the top women's prize for her 17th-place finish.
The top 10 finishers in the second tournament.
Third Tournament: Martinez Just Shy Of Perfect Performance

The third tournament was a one-man show from start to finish, featuring the now-16-time winner Martinez. 10 consecutive victories left him on the brink of achieving the first perfect score in 3 0 Thursday history. However, a tough loss on the black side of the Queen's Pawn Opening: Levitsky Attack at the hands of Terry denied him the accolade.
Terry spoiled the perfect points party. Photo: Renato Terry.
Martinez's earlier games stood out due to his lightning pace and incisive sacrifices. In round 10, he punched a hole in Fedoseev's kingside with the delectable 18.Nxe6!!.
Wins over GMs Sina Movahed, Volodar Murzin, and IM Yoseph Taher further underlined the dominance of his performance.
Martinez knocked over 3000+ rated blitzers like bowling pins. Photo: Chess.com.

Martinez wasn't the only player racking up brilliancies, though. The top-scoring women's player, Bulgarian IM Nurgyul Salimova, climbed to 12th place after uncorking a sacrifice that directed the game toward a winning rook ending.
When the dust settled, Martinez finished first with 10/11, Movahed in second on 9/11, and GM Nguyen Ngoc Truong Son in third with 8.5/11.
The top 10 finishers in the third tournament.

3 0 Thursday is a set of three weekly Swiss tournaments for verified titled players featuring their favorite time control. Each of the three tournaments is an 11-round Swiss with a 3+0 time control. The combined prize fund is $3,000 every week.
